config.title: Build typed tree node structure

intro.title: Build typed tree node structure
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a typed tree node structure using TypeScript. You will create a generic TreeNode class that can store data of any type and maintain references to its child nodes. This introduces the core concept of recursive data structures, where a type can contain references to instances of itself. You will use TypeScript's generic types to ensure type safety and interfaces to define the structure. By the end, you will have a reusable, type-safe tree implementation.
intro.usecase: A typed tree node structure is essential for building complex, nested UI components in real-world applications. For example, file explorers in IDEs like VS Code, navigation menus in dashboards, and hierarchical data displays in admin panels all rely on this pattern. As a developer, you'll use typed trees to manage component state in design systems, render dynamic form sections, or build interactive data visualizations where parent-child relationships must be strictly enforced. Implementing this with TypeScript ensures your UI logic is robust, maintainable, and free from runtime errors when dealing with nested data.

objectives: Construct a TypeScript interface to define the structure of a tree node with typed properties
Implement a class that enforces the tree node interface with proper type annotations
Initialize tree node instances with typed data values and nested children arrays
Manipulate the tree structure by adding and removing child nodes with type safety
Configure recursive methods to traverse the typed tree structure
Apply generic types to create reusable tree node structures for different data types
Integrate type guards to validate node properties during tree operations

steps.title: Import TypeScript type definitions
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript file and import nothing (this is a pure TypeScript lesson, no framework imports needed).
steps.hint: Since this is a pure TypeScript lesson without any framework, you don't need to import any external libraries or modules. Just create a clean TypeScript file.

// Pure TypeScript file with no imports

steps.expectedOutcome: A clean TypeScript file ready for building typed tree node structures without any external dependencies.
successCriteria: File contains no import statements and is ready for pure TypeScript development.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but remember this is a pure TypeScript lesson. Make sure you haven't imported any external libraries or frameworks.

steps.title: Define TreeNode interface with basic properties
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named TreeNode with two properties: value of type number and children of type TreeNode[].
steps.hint: Use the interface keyword followed by the interface name and the property definitions inside curly braces.
steps.expectedOutcome: A TreeNode interface is defined with the correct property types, ready to be used as a type for tree nodes.
successCriteria: The TreeNode interface exists with value: number and children: TreeNode[] properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your interface has both value (number) and children (TreeNode[]) properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Check that you used the interface keyword and defined both properties with the correct types.

steps.title: Add optional id property to TreeNode interface
steps.instruction: Add an optional id property of type string to your TreeNode interface definition.
steps.hint: In TypeScript, you can make a property optional by adding a question mark (?) after its name in the interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: The TreeNode interface should have an optional id property that can store string identifiers for tree nodes.
successCriteria: TreeNode interface includes an optional id property of type string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the id property is optional (using ?) and has the correct type (string).
steps.feedbackWrong: The TreeNode interface should have an optional id property of type string. Check the syntax for optional properties in TypeScript interfaces.

steps.title: Create a typed tree node instance
steps.instruction: Create a constant named rootNode that implements the TreeNode interface with sample data. Use a value of 10 and an id of 'root'.
steps.hint: Define a constant with the type annotation TreeNode and assign an object with the required properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: A rootNode constant is created with the correct type and sample data.
successCriteria: rootNode is a constant of type TreeNode with value 10 and id 'root'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure rootNode has the correct type annotation and includes both value and id properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The rootNode constant doesn't match the expected structure. Check that it implements TreeNode with value: 10 and id: 'root'.

steps.title: Define a function to create tree nodes
steps.instruction: Define a function named 'createTreeNode' that takes a number value and returns a TreeNode object with that value and a generated id.
steps.hint: Create a function that accepts a number parameter and returns an object matching the TreeNode interface. You can generate a simple id using Date.now() or Math.random().
steps.expectedOutcome: A createTreeNode function that produces TreeNode objects with proper TypeScript typing.
successCriteria: The createTreeNode function is defined, accepts a number parameter, returns a TreeNode object with value and id properties, and has appropriate type annotations.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function accepts a number parameter and returns an object with both value and id properties that match the TreeNode interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function definition doesn't match the requirements. It should be named createTreeNode, accept a number, and return a TreeNode object with value and id properties.

steps.title: Use the factory function to create child nodes
steps.instruction: Use the createTreeNode function to create two child nodes and add them to the rootNode's children array.
steps.hint: Call createTreeNode with appropriate values and push them into the children array of rootNode.
steps.expectedOutcome: Two child nodes are created using createTreeNode and added to rootNode's children array.
successCriteria: rootNode.children contains two child nodes created with createTreeNode.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you call createTreeNode to create the child nodes and push them into rootNode.children.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're using createTreeNode to create the child nodes and adding them to rootNode.children.

steps.title: Define a generic TreeNode interface
steps.instruction: Create a new interface called GenericTreeNode<T> that uses TypeScript generics. It should have a generic 'value' property of type T, and optional 'id' (number) and 'children' (array of GenericTreeNode<T>) properties.
steps.hint: Start with 'interface GenericTreeNode<T> {'. The value property should be typed as T. Keep the same optional id and children structure as the existing TreeNode interface, but make children use GenericTreeNode<T>[].
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a GenericTreeNode<T> interface that can represent tree nodes with values of any type, while maintaining the same structure.
successCriteria: The GenericTreeNode<T> interface is defined with a generic value property, optional id (number), and optional children (GenericTreeNode<T>[]).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your GenericTreeNode<T> interface has: 1) A generic 'value' property of type T, 2) Optional 'id' property of type number, and 3) Optional 'children' property that's an array of GenericTreeNode<T>.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create an interface called GenericTreeNode<T> with a value property of type T, an optional id of type number, and optional children that's an array of GenericTreeNode<T>.

steps.title: Create a generic tree node instance
steps.instruction: Create a constant named stringTreeNode using the GenericTreeNode interface with string as the type argument, and assign it an object with value 'hello', id 2, and an empty children array.
steps.hint: Use the GenericTreeNode<string> type annotation for the constant, then create an object with the required properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a constant stringTreeNode that is explicitly typed as GenericTreeNode<string> with the required properties.
successCriteria: The constant stringTreeNode is declared with type GenericTreeNode<string> and has value 'hello', id 2, and children [].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure stringTreeNode is explicitly typed as GenericTreeNode<string> and has all required properties: value 'hello', id 2, and children [].
steps.feedbackWrong: The constant stringTreeNode is missing or incorrectly typed. It should be of type GenericTreeNode<string> with value 'hello', id 2, and children [].

steps.title: Define a recursive tree traversal function
steps.instruction: Create a function named traverseTree that accepts a TreeNode parameter and recursively processes all nodes by logging their values.
steps.hint: Define a function that takes a TreeNode as a parameter. Inside, log the node's value, then loop through its children array (if it exists) and call traverseTree recursively on each child.
steps.expectedOutcome: A traverseTree function is defined that logs node values and recursively processes children.
successCriteria: The traverseTree function is defined with a TreeNode parameter, logs node values, and recursively calls itself for child nodes.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function accepts a TreeNode parameter, logs the value, and recursively calls itself for any children.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a function named traverseTree that takes a TreeNode and recursively logs all node values.

steps.title: Test the typed tree structure
steps.instruction: Call the traverseTree function with the rootNode and log the results to verify the typed tree structure works correctly.
steps.hint: Use console.log to output the result of calling traverseTree with rootNode as the argument.
steps.expectedOutcome: The typed tree structure is verified by logging the traversal results, confirming type safety and structure correctness.
successCriteria: traverseTree is called with rootNode and the results are logged using console.log.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're calling traverseTree with rootNode as the argument and logging the results using console.log.
steps.feedbackWrong: call the traverseTree function with rootNode and log the results to verify the typed tree structure.
